section.title: Wisdom Builds, Folly Destroys
section.sectionRationale: One of the longest chapters in the collection, gathering sayings on building and tearing down, verses 1 to 7, folly's self deception and the way that seems right, verses 8 to 14, prudence and kindness to the poor, verses 15 to 21, honest labor and the fear of the LORD as a fountain of life, verses 22 to 28, and patience, a tranquil heart, and a nation's true exaltation, verses 29 to 35.
section.thesis: Wisdom quietly builds a house, a life, and a nation, while folly, often through paths that feel entirely right from the inside, just as quietly tears them down, and only the fear of the LORD reliably tells the two apart.
section.frameNote: Five thematic clusters of seven verses each: building and tearing down, verses 1 to 7; folly's self deception and the way that seems right, verses 8 to 14; prudence and kindness to the poor, verses 15 to 21; honest labor and the fear of the LORD as a fountain of life, verses 22 to 28; and patience, a tranquil heart, and a nation's true exaltation, verses 29 to 35.

verses.text: Every wise woman {{banah|builds}} her house, but a foolish one tears it down with her own hands.
He who walks in uprightness fears the LORD, but the one who is devious in his ways despises Him.
The proud speech of a fool brings a rod to his back, but the lips of the wise protect them.
Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty, but an abundant harvest comes through the strength of the ox.
An honest witness does not deceive, but a dishonest witness pours forth lies.
A mocker seeks wisdom and finds none, but knowledge comes easily to the discerning.
Stay away from a foolish man; you will gain no knowledge from his speech.
The wisdom of the prudent is to discern his way, but the folly of fools deceives them.
Fools mock the making of amends, but goodwill is found among the upright.
The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares in its joy.
The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish.
There is a {{derek|way}} that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death.
Even in laughter the heart may ache, and joy may end in sorrow.
The backslider in heart receives the fill of his own ways, but a good man is rewarded for his ways.

units.label: Prudence and kindness to the poor
units.note: watching your steps and your neighbor

verses.text: The simple man believes every word, but the prudent man watches his steps.
A wise man fears and turns from evil, but a fool is careless and reckless.
A quick-tempered man acts foolishly, and a devious man is hated.
The simple inherit folly, but the prudent are crowned with knowledge.
The evil bow before the good, and the wicked at the gates of the righteous.
The poor man is hated even by his neighbor, but many are those who love the rich.
He who despises his neighbor sins, but blessed is he who shows {{chanan|kindness}} to the poor.

units.label: Honest labor and the fountain of life
units.note: the fear of the LORD, again

verses.text: Do not those who contrive evil go astray? But those who plan goodness find loving devotion and faithfulness.
There is profit in all labor, but mere talk leads only to poverty.
The crown of the wise is their wealth, but the effort of fools is folly.
A truthful witness saves lives, but one who utters lies is deceitful.
He who fears the LORD is secure in confidence, and his children shall have a place of refuge.
The {{yirah|fear of the LORD}} is a fountain of life, turning a man from the snares of death.
A large population is a king's splendor, but a lack of subjects is a prince's ruin.

units.label: Patience, a tranquil heart, and a nation exalted

verses.text: A patient man has great understanding, but a quick-tempered man promotes folly.
A tranquil heart is life to the body, but envy rots the bones.
Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker, but whoever is kind to the needy honors Him.
The wicked man is thrown down by his own sin, but the righteous man has a refuge even in death.
Wisdom rests in the heart of the discerning; even among fools she is known.
Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a disgrace to any people.
A king delights in a wise servant, but his anger falls on the shameful.

banah.gloss: To build, used in verse 1 of the wise woman who builds her house, set against the foolish woman who tears hers down with her own hands. The verb pictures wisdom and folly not as abstract qualities but as ongoing, active work with lasting structural consequences.

derek.gloss: Way or path, used in verse 12's warning that a way can seem right to a person and still end in death. The same line reappears nearly word for word at 16:25, making it one of the book's most emphatic warnings against trusting one's own inner sense of rightness above God's revealed wisdom.

chanan.gloss: To show favor, grace, or kindness, used in verse 21 of kindness shown to the poor, called a blessing in deliberate contrast to the sin of despising one's neighbor. The same root describes God's own gracious favor throughout the Old Testament, tying human kindness to the poor to the character of God Himself.

yirah.gloss: The fear of the LORD, called a fountain of life in verse 27, using imagery identical to 13:14's fountain of wise teaching, and tying this whole chapter's many contrasts of wisdom and folly back to the book's foundational reverence for God.

basic.context: This long chapter surveys wisdom and folly across household, workplace, courtroom, and nation. A wise woman builds her house while a foolish one tears hers down with her own hands. A path can feel entirely right and still lead to death. Kindness to the poor honors the very God who made them, while oppressing them is nothing less than taunting their Maker. And a whole nation, not just an individual, is exalted by righteousness or disgraced by sin.
basic.hermeneutics: As elsewhere in this collection, these are independent, largely antithetic proverbs, but this chapter's sheer length allows several themes to be explored from multiple angles, folly's self deception, verses 8 to 14, prudence toward the poor, verses 15 to 21, and the fear of the LORD as life's true foundation, verses 26 to 27. Verse 12's warning is especially important for reading the whole book rightly, a path's felt rightness is not proof of its actual rightness; only revealed wisdom, rooted in the fear of the LORD, can be fully trusted.
basic.originalLanguages: Banah, to build, verse 1, pictures wisdom and folly as ongoing construction or demolition, not static traits. Derek, way, verse 12, names a path that can feel right while still ending in death, a warning repeated nearly verbatim at 16:25. Chanan, to show kindness or favor, verse 21, links kindness toward the poor to the same gracious character elsewhere used of God's own favor. And yirah, the fear of the LORD, verse 27, is called a fountain of life, echoing 13:14's fountain of wise teaching.
basic.typology: Verse 31's claim that oppressing the poor taunts their Maker, while kindness to them honors Him, anticipates Christ's own teaching that whatever is done to the least of these is done to Him personally, Matthew 25:40, 45, showing that God identifies Himself with the poor and needy in a way this proverb had already glimpsed.
basic.christ: Verse 12's warning, that a way can seem right to a person and still end in death, exposes humanity's need for a wisdom beyond its own inner sense of rightness, a need met fully in Christ, who alone is the way, the truth, and the life, John 14:6, the one path that truly leads where it feels it should. And verse 31's claim that kindness to the needy honors God Himself is deepened immeasurably by Christ's own words that whatever is done for the least of His brothers is done for Him, Matthew 25:40, showing that God's identification with the poor is not incidental but personal, ultimately embodied in the incarnate Christ.
basic.god: God is the one whose fear grounds a truly secure life and a fountain of life itself, verses 26 to 27, and He is personally invested in how the poor are treated, taking their mistreatment as an insult to Himself and their care as an honor to Himself, verse 31. He also governs whole nations, not merely individuals, exalting or disgracing them according to righteousness or sin, verse 34.
basic.crossReferences: Proverbs 16:25 repeats verse 12 nearly word for word, reinforcing its warning. Matthew 25:40, 45 has Christ identify Himself with the poor and needy, echoing verse 31. John 14:6 presents Christ as the way that truly leads to life, the answer to the false way of verse 12. Galatians 6:9 encourages perseverance in doing good, related to the fruit of patient understanding in verse 29.
basic.oneStory: This chapter's picture of wisdom quietly building and folly quietly tearing down, of paths that feel right yet end in death, and of God's own investment in how the poor are treated, belongs to Scripture's ongoing story of the two ways and the God who governs both individuals and nations. That story reaches its resolution in Christ, the one true way to life, who identifies Himself so fully with the poor that kindness to them is kindness to Him.

context.literary:
Proverbs 14 is the longest chapter in the first Solomonic collection, and it is held together by images of building, paths and refuge. Verse 1 opens with a house that is built or torn down by a woman's own hands. Verse 35 closes with a king and his servants, so that the chapter moves from the smallest household to the court. In between, the LORD is named only in verses 2, 26 and 27. Verse 2 starts the thread with the man whose uprightness shows that he fears the LORD, while verses 26 and 27 gather it into a pair: the fear of the LORD is 'secure in confidence', a refuge for children, and 'a fountain of life'.

A theme of appearance against reality runs through the first half. The prudent man discerns his way while the fool is deceived by his own folly, verse 8. The heart knows its bitterness, though no stranger can see it, verse 10. A way seems right but ends in death, verse 12. Laughter hides an aching heart, verse 13. The simple believe everything they hear, verse 15. Each saying asks the reader not to trust what a thing looks like.

The second half turns outward. Verses 20 and 21 and verse 31 flank the middle with the poor and their neighbours. Verses 23 and 24 treat labour and its reward. Verse 25 sets a truthful witness who saves lives beside the liar. Verses 28 to 35 widen to king, temper, envy, death, nation and court. The tone moves from private discernment to public consequence, and the central claim is that character shapes a household and then a nation.

The chapter also contains a strikingly honest note in verse 10, which admits that no one fully shares another's inner life. It is a reminder that this book of wisdom knows its limits.
context.historical:
The 'house' of verse 1 meant more than a building. In Israel a house was a family line, which is why the elders at Ruth's wedding pray that the woman entering the home will be like Rachel and Leah, 'who together built up the house of Israel,' Ruth 4:11. A woman who builds a house is raising children, running resources and shaping the name of the family. The tearing down by 'her own hands' could be waste, quarrels or neglect, and no outside enemy was needed.

Verse 4 comes straight from the farm. Oxen supplied the plough and the threshing, so a clean manger meant no animals and no harvest. The sage observes that strength comes at the cost of mess, and that tidy emptiness is not wisdom.

The witnesses of verses 5 and 25 stand in a legal world where trials were decided by neighbours' testimony at the gate. A truthful witness could save an innocent man's life and a false witness could take it, so the saying is literally about life and death.

The poor man hated by his neighbour in verse 20 lived in a society driven by patronage and social ties. A person without land or kin had little protection, and James still describes the habit of honouring the rich and dishonouring the poor, James 2:2-6.

Verses 28 and 35 belong to royal court wisdom. A large population meant labour, taxes and soldiers, and a king depended on capable servants such as Joseph and Daniel. The tent and the house in verse 11 reflect Israel's memory of tent life: the modest tent of the upright outlasts the stately house of the wicked.
context.canonical:
Verse 1 connects with Wisdom who 'has built her house' in Proverbs 9:1 and with the elders' blessing in Ruth 4:11. The Bible's building language then widens: Jesus tells of a wise builder who hears and acts, Matthew 7:24, Hebrews says 'God is the builder of everything,' Hebrews 3:4, and Paul and Peter picture the church as a house grown from Christ the cornerstone and built of living stones, Ephesians 2:20-22 and 1 Peter 2:5.

Verse 12 repeats in Proverbs 16:25 and sits with Proverbs 21:2, 'All a man's ways seem right to him, but the LORD weighs the heart,' and with the refrain at the end of Judges, where everyone did what was right in his own eyes, Judges 21:25. Paul stands behind it as a witness: 'they are zealous for God, but not on the basis of knowledge,' Romans 10:2, and he confesses of his own past, 'I was convinced that I ought to do all I could to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth,' Acts 26:9.

Verse 15 is picked up in the apostolic instruction, 'do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits,' 1 John 4:1, and in the praise of the Bereans who examined the Scriptures every day, Acts 17:11.

Verses 26 and 27 link to the book's motto, 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge,' Proverbs 1:7, and to the fountain of life in Psalm 36:9. Verse 29 draws on the LORD's self-description as 'slow to anger,' Exodus 34:6. Verse 31 parallels Proverbs 17:5 and 19:17, and Jesus gives it its fullest form in Matthew 25:40 and 45. Verse 34 stands near Psalm 33:12 and Deuteronomy 4:6, which holds that Israel's obedience would show the nations its wisdom.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants the hearer to be a builder. The opening image of a house put up or pulled down by choices presents each reader with an ongoing task, and every saying that follows is a piece of the craft: how to speak, whom to trust, how to treat a neighbour, what to do with temper, and how to see through a flattering path.

A second purpose is to make the hearer suspicious of his own certainty. The warnings in verses 8, 12 and 15 are directed at a young man who is confident in his judgment. The author does not ask him to abandon thinking. He asks him to examine his steps, to watch where a road ends and to look for the voice that corrects him. Wisdom here is the habit of asking 'where does this lead?'

The sage also wants the hearer to treat the poor as people with a Maker. In a world that loved the rich and hated the poor, verse 31 makes a bold theological claim that changes how the poor must be seen. Kindness is not charity from above but honour offered to God.

Finally, he intends to ground it all in the fear of the LORD. Verses 26 and 27 are the heart of the chapter. Without that fear, building, discernment and kindness are just techniques. With it, they become a way of life under a God who gives refuge and life.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter contains both direct instruction and observed reality, and the difference matters. 'Stay away from a foolish man,' verse 7, is a command with a stated reason. Kindness to the poor, verse 21, and patience, verse 29, are things the hearer is told to practise. Verse 15 sets the simple man who believes everything against the prudent who watches his steps, and the implied instruction is to be the second.

Other verses only observe. Verse 20, 'The poor man is hated even by his neighbor, but many are those who love the rich,' does not approve of the habit. It records it, with a sad accuracy that the next verse corrects by calling contempt for a neighbour a sin. Verse 28 on a large population being a king's splendour is a statement about ancient kingship, not a policy recommendation or a verdict on every nation's size. Verse 4 observes that productive work is untidy, and it does not tell the reader to prefer a mess.

Verse 12 deserves special care. It does not teach that every sincere conviction is false or that conscience should be ignored. It warns that feeling right is not the same as being right, and it directs the reader to the standard outside himself. Verse 7 also needs balance, for it advises distance from a persistent fool and does not forbid showing him kindness, as Jesus did with sinners, Matthew 11:19. The right use of the chapter is to take its warnings as a mirror and its encouragements as a call to build.

debates.question: What does verse 12 say about the reliability of human conscience and reasoning?

views.label: It warns against self-deceived conviction that has not submitted to God's word
views.case: The saying appears twice, here and in Proverbs 16:25, both times among sayings about fools, mockers and the fear of the LORD. Paul's life gives a clear example: he was 'convinced' that he ought to oppose the name of Jesus, Acts 26:9, and he later said his people were zealous but 'not on the basis of knowledge,' Romans 10:2. The failure was not a lack of sincerity but a lack of submission to revelation.

views.label: It warns more broadly that unaided human judgment is limited
views.case: Jeremiah says that 'the heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure,' Jeremiah 17:9, and Proverbs 21:2 says that all of a man's ways seem right to him, 'but the LORD weighs the heart.' On this reading the verse is a general statement about human fallibility, true even of those who mean well.

debates.bearing: Both readings lead to the same practice: test the felt rightness of a path against the word of God and the counsel of the wise, and fear the LORD, as verse 27 says. The verse is not hostile to thinking. It is hostile to the idea that a feeling of certainty settles the matter.

debates.question: What does 'Fools mock the making of amends' in verse 9 mean?

views.label: Fools treat reconciliation and making amends as a joke
views.case: The BSB takes the Hebrew word asham in the sense of reparation or compensation. A fool scoffs at the idea of putting a wrong right, while goodwill is found among the upright. This fits the surrounding sayings about fools who laugh at what the wise take seriously.

views.label: Fools make light of the guilt offering
views.case: Asham is the technical name of the guilt offering in the law, where a person who had wronged the LORD or a neighbour brought an offering and made restitution, Leviticus 5:15 and 6:6. Some read the line as fools mocking the very means of reparation that God provided. The second line, about favour among the upright, then sets this against those who take guilt seriously.

debates.bearing: The line is terse and translators differ, so no reading should be pressed too hard. Both agree that the fool laughs at guilt and the cost of putting things right. In the light of Isaiah 53:10, where the Servant's soul is made a guilt offering, the second reading gains a New Testament resonance, though the proverb itself is making a general point.

debates.question: What is the 'refuge even in death' of verse 32?

views.label: A hope that reaches beyond death
views.case: The Hebrew text, which the BSB follows, says the righteous man has a refuge in his death. Psalm 73:24 speaks of being received in glory, and Paul says to depart is to be with Christ, Philippians 1:23. Many readers see here an early glimpse of a hope that death does not end God's care.

views.label: A refuge in his integrity
views.case: Some modern translations follow ancient versions and read 'in his integrity' where the Hebrew has 'in his death'. On this reading the verse is about the security that uprightness gives in life, contrasting with the wicked who are thrown down by their own sin.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew text as it stands is the better guide, and it fits the New Testament's hope. Even if the other reading is chosen, the chapter has already said that the fear of the LORD is a refuge, verse 26, and that it turns a man from the snares of death, verse 27.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verse uses a plural noun that English cannot show. The BSB reads 'Every wise woman', but the Hebrew has the plural chokhmot, 'wisdoms', joined to 'women'. The same plural form is used of Wisdom herself in Proverbs 1:20 and 9:1, where she 'has built her house'. The echo is deliberate: the wise woman does in her home what Wisdom does in the world, and the foolish woman unbuilds it.

In verse 9 the key word is asham, which means guilt and also the guilt offering and reparation. It is the word for the offering a person brought when he had acted unfaithfully, Leviticus 5:15, with an unblemished ram of proper value. It is also the word of Isaiah 53:10, where the Servant's soul is made a guilt offering. Fools who mock 'asham' are laughing at the whole matter of guilt and repair.

Verse 29 contrasts the 'patient' and the 'quick-tempered' with two vivid phrases. The patient man is literally 'long of nostrils', erekh appayim, the idiom for slow anger, and it is the very phrase Exodus 34:6 uses of the LORD: 'slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness.' The quick-tempered man is literally 'short of spirit', qetsar ruach. Patience here is not a mere temperament but a share in the character of God.

In verse 31 the verb 'taunts' is cherep, 'to reproach' or 'to insult', and it is the verb behind Proverbs 17:5, 'He who mocks the poor insults their Maker.' To mistreat the poor is to reproach the One who made them. The Maker here is a participle of 'asah, the work-word, which also lies behind Proverbs 22:2: 'The LORD is Maker of them all.'

Verse 30 says envy 'rots the bones'. The Hebrew uses the noun rakav, 'rot' or 'decay', the same word as in Proverbs 12:4, where a shameful wife is 'like decay in his bones'. The deep damage in both is internal, hidden from sight.

Verse 34 ends with a twist. The BSB reads 'sin is a disgrace to any people', but the Hebrew word is chesed, the same word that elsewhere is the usual term for loyal love, as in verse 22: 'loving devotion and faithfulness.' In this verse it is a rare homonym meaning reproach or disgrace, as in Leviticus 20:17.

Finally, in verse 33 the BSB notes that the Hebrew says wisdom is known even among fools, while the Greek and Syriac versions read 'but among fools she is not known'. The Hebrew makes a surprising claim, that wisdom is recognised even among fools.

typology.type: The house built by wisdom, Proverbs 14:1
typology.fulfillment: Wisdom builds a house, and Proverbs 9:1 pictures Wisdom herself building hers. Jesus is the builder of a house greater than Moses', 'just as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house itself,' Hebrews 3:3. He says, 'on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it,' Matthew 16:18. The church is 'fitted together' in Him as a holy temple, Ephesians 2:21, and believers are 'living stones,' 1 Peter 2:5. The proverb gives each family a task of building; Christ is the one who builds what no family could, a house that endures. The type falls short because human builders can only do their part on a foundation already laid.

typology.type: The way that seems right and the Way, Proverbs 14:12
typology.fulfillment: The proverb sets one deceptive road against others, and the Bible keeps the image of two ways, as in Matthew 7:13-14 where the broad way leads to destruction and the narrow one to life. Jesus makes himself the road: 'I am the way and the truth and the life,' John 14:6. The early church was known simply as 'the Way,' Acts 9:2 and 24:14. The correspondence is real, and it is also a deepening: the proverb warns that some roads end in death, while Christ goes down the road of death and returns, so that the way can be walked by people who do not know the way.

typology.type: The Maker among the poor, Proverbs 14:31
typology.fulfillment: To oppress the poor is to taunt their Maker, and kindness honours Him. The Maker of the poor then came among them. Jesus was laid in a manger, Luke 2:7, preached good news to the poor, Luke 4:18, and was one who 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. He identified Himself with the least: 'whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me,' Matthew 25:40. The proverb's link is that God made the poor. In Christ the link is deeper, since the Maker has taken their condition on himself. The type falls short because a proverb can only say that God cares, while the incarnation shows how far.

typology.type: The righteous with a refuge in death, Proverbs 14:32
typology.fulfillment: The righteous man has a refuge even in death. Christ shows what that refuge is. He died with the words, 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit,' Luke 23:46, and He 'abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel,' 2 Timothy 1:10. Because He went before, David's confidence, 'Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me,' Psalm 23:4, becomes Paul's, 'to die is gain,' Philippians 1:21. The proverb gives a promise of shelter; Christ is the shelter, and He has passed through death to the other side.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first as builder. Verse 1 sets a house built or torn down, and the New Testament tells us who builds the house that matters. 'I will build My church,' Jesus says, Matthew 16:18, and Hebrews adds that the builder of a house has greater honour than the house, Hebrews 3:3. Where a family can be torn down from within, the church built by Christ is held by 'the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.'

It leads to Christ as the Way. Verse 12 warns of a road that seems right and ends in death. Jesus does not simply point at a better road; He says, 'I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me,' John 14:6. Paul is a case study in verse 12: sincere, zealous and wrong, until Christ met him on the road. The proverb's warning is thus answered by a person who stands on the road and calls travellers to follow.

It leads to Christ as the Maker of the poor. Verse 31 ties kindness to the needy with honour to their Maker, and Jesus carries the thought to its end: 'whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me,' and 'whatever you did not do for one of the least of these, you did not do for Me,' Matthew 25:40 and 45. The one who judges is the one who became poor, 2 Corinthians 8:9, and who came 'to preach good news to the poor,' Luke 4:18.

It leads to Christ as the patient one. Verse 29 praises the man who is slow to anger. That is the character of God described at Sinai, Exodus 34:6, and Paul sees it in Christ's dealings with him: 'Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience as an example,' 1 Timothy 1:16.

It leads to Christ as the true witness. Verse 25 says a truthful witness saves lives. Jesus 'made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate,' 1 Timothy 6:13, and told Pilate that He had come 'to testify to the truth,' John 18:37. The envy that rots the bones in verse 30 was behind His trial: Pilate 'knew it was out of envy that they had handed Jesus over,' Matthew 27:18. The truthful witness saved lives by dying, which verse 25 could not foresee.

It leads to Christ as the servant in whom the King delights. Verse 35 says a king delights in a wise servant. The Father says of the Servant in Isaiah, 'My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights,' Isaiah 42:1, and of the Messiah in Isaiah 11:3, 'He will delight in the fear of the LORD,' which verses 26 and 27 call a fountain of life. And the refuge in death of verse 32 is made firm because He has walked through death and risen.

As always, some caution is needed. The ox, the manger, the laughing heart and the king's census are not hidden pictures of Christ. The links above stand because the New Testament draws them or because the chapter's central themes of building, the way, the poor and the fear of the LORD meet in Him.
study.god:
The centre of the chapter is the fear of the LORD, and what it says about God is summed up in verses 26 and 27. To fear Him is to be 'secure in confidence' and to give one's children 'a place of refuge'. God is the shelter of those who revere Him. He is also 'a fountain of life, turning a man from the snares of death', so He is the source from which wisdom, safety and life flow. The fear here is not terror but a trust that bows to the one who is both awesome and kind.

He is Maker of the poor and of the rich. Verse 31 stakes a claim on the poor man's behalf: to oppress him is to taunt his Maker, and kindness honours God Himself. The God of this chapter is therefore not neutral about social position. He has made each person, and He treats an insult to the least as an insult to Himself. Proverbs 22:2 repeats the claim: 'The rich and the poor have this in common: The LORD is Maker of them all.'

He is patient. Verse 29 praises the slow to anger, and Exodus 34:6 shows that patience is how God describes Himself. Psalm 103:8 repeats it: 'The LORD is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion.' Verse 22 uses the pair of words that Exodus 34:6 gives for His character, 'loving devotion and faithfulness', and says that those who plan goodness find these. People who plan good discover that they are walking with the grain of the character of God.

He knows what no one else can see. Verse 10 admits that no stranger shares the heart's bitterness or joy, and verse 13 admits that laughter can hide an ache. God is the one who sees past appearances: 'the LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart,' 1 Samuel 16:7. In Jesus He also sympathises: 'we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses,' Hebrews 4:15.

He governs nations. Verse 34 says righteousness exalts a nation, and sin is a disgrace to any people. The God of Proverbs is not only the God of the private conscience. He deals with peoples, and Psalm 33:12 calls blessed the nation whose God is the LORD.

The chapter holds a tension that every reader meets. God ordains a moral order in which the wicked house is destroyed and the upright tent flourishes, verse 11, yet verse 12 admits that a path can seem right and still end in death, and verse 20 admits that the poor are hated. God's justice is not always plain on the surface. The refuge of verse 32, even in death, says that the final word lies beyond what can be seen.

For worship, the chapter asks us to fear the LORD in the way that finds security, to thank Him for being Maker of the humblest, to imitate His patience, and to bring our hidden hearts to the one who sees them.

crossReferences.note: 'Wisdom has built her house; she has carved out her seven pillars.' The chapter's opening line about a wise woman who builds echoes this larger picture of Wisdom as builder, and it suggests that every household which builds wisely is joining a work that Wisdom herself began.

The elders bless Boaz's bride, praying that she will be like Rachel and Leah, 'who together built up the house of Israel.' It shows that building a house was the highest praise for a woman in Israel, and it gives verse 1 a concrete example in the family line that led to David.

A wise man builds his house on the rock and it stands through rain and wind. Jesus turns the proverb about building into a test of hearing and doing His words. The difference between the two houses is not the weather but the foundation.

The saying repeats verse 12 word for word, 'There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death.' Its placement among the sayings about a king's decrees and the LORD's weighing of motives sharpens the warning: self-confidence is hazardous without God's verdict.

Paul says of his fellow Israelites that they are 'zealous for God, but not on the basis of knowledge.' It is verse 12 in a living case: sincere religious devotion on a path that does not lead where it hopes. The cure is the righteousness that comes from God, not more zeal.

'Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God.' John turns the simple man's gullibility in verse 15 into a church discipline. Prudence is applied to teaching, and the standard for testing is what the Spirit and the apostles have given.

When the LORD passes before Moses He declares Himself 'slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness.' Verses 22 and 29 draw on these same words, which shows that the human virtues praised in the chapter are reflections of God's own self-revelation.

'He who mocks the poor insults their Maker.' The saying uses the same verb as verse 31, with a second warning that whoever gloats over calamity will not go unpunished. The repetition shows that the link between the poor and their Maker was a settled conviction among the sages.

'Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me.' Jesus gives verse 31 a face. The Maker of the poor is now the judge who counts kindness to them as kindness to Himself, and the proverb's principle becomes the standard of the last day.

James describes a meeting where a man with a gold ring is honoured and a poor man in shabby clothes is dismissed, and says, 'you have dishonored the poor.' He treats the habit of verse 20 as sin, and he adds that God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith.

'Every house is built by someone, but God is the builder of everything.' The writer takes the image of a built house, which verse 1 uses for a family, and lifts it to the whole created and redeemed order, with Christ as the builder who deserves greater honour than the house.

Paul says that to live is Christ and to die is gain, and that he desires to depart and be with Christ. It is a New Testament voice answering verse 32, where the righteous has a refuge even in death. For Paul the refuge has a name and a presence.

'Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people He has chosen as His inheritance!' This psalm gives the positive side of verse 34. A nation is exalted not by its numbers or strength but by the God it serves and the righteousness that follows.

study.oneStory:
Proverbs 14 is a chapter of building and roads, and Scripture's story begins with both. God made the world and then planted a garden, and He placed humanity in it as His work to tend, with a Maker over rich and poor alike. The first road that seemed right was taken in Eden: the woman 'saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes, and that it was desirable for obtaining wisdom,' Genesis 3:6. Everything looked right, and the end was death. Verse 12 is the sage's summary of the oldest mistake.

After the fall, the story is a contest between houses and ways. Israel is called to be a nation whose righteousness exalts it, and the Law holds that its obedience will show the nations its wisdom, Deuteronomy 4:6. The book of Judges closes with the opposite: 'everyone did what was right in his own eyes,' Judges 21:25. The kings come and go, some delighting in wise servants, as Pharaoh did in Joseph, and some turning on the shameful. The prophets summon Israel to see that what seems right has led to the disgrace of a people, and the exile is the house torn down.

The turn comes in Christ. He is the builder, the Way, the Maker who became poor, the patient one, the truthful witness and the Servant in whom the Father delights. In Him a household of faith is built from Jew and Gentile, 'with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone,' Ephesians 2:20, and the people of the Way are called by the name of the road. In a world that loves the rich, the church is told to 'remember the poor,' Galatians 2:10, because the poor have a Maker who has been among them.

Until the end the church lives in the tension the chapter names: a path can look right, a heart can hide its pain, the poor can be hated, and death still comes. Believers test the spirits, wait patiently, pursue kindness and take refuge in the fear of the LORD.

The ending is a house and a city. Jesus says, 'In My Father's house are many rooms,' John 14:2, and the vision of Revelation is of God's dwelling with man, Revelation 21:3. The kings of the earth bring their glory into it, Revelation 21:24, so nations are at last exalted by righteousness. The fountain of life flows freely, Revelation 21:6, and the refuge that Proverbs glimpsed in death becomes a home without death.

quiz.q: What image does verse 1 use to describe wisdom and folly in the home?

options.text: A wise woman builds her house, while a foolish one tears it down with her own hands.
options.note: This is the exact image and contrast given.

options.text: Both wise and foolish women build equally strong households.
options.note: The verse draws a sharp contrast, not equal outcomes.

options.text: Only men are responsible for building a household in this proverb.
options.note: The proverb specifically addresses a woman's active role in building or tearing down the house.

options.text: Foolishness only affects the household's finances, not its structure or stability.
options.note: The image of tearing down 'with her own hands' suggests a broader, active destruction, not narrowly financial.

quiz.q: What warning does verse 12 give, and where else does it appear in Proverbs?

options.text: A way can seem right to a person yet end in death, a warning repeated nearly word for word at 16:25.
options.note: This exact repetition signals the warning's special importance.

options.text: Feeling confident about a decision always guarantees it is correct.
options.note: The verse warns precisely against trusting felt rightness as proof of a path's actual safety.

options.text: It appears only once in the entire book, with no repetition.
options.note: The verse is repeated almost verbatim later, at 16:25.

options.text: It is a warning specifically about financial investments.
options.note: The warning is general, about any path in life, not limited to financial decisions.

quiz.q: According to verse 31, what does oppressing the poor amount to?

options.text: Taunting their Maker, while kindness to the needy honors Him.
options.note: This is the exact and striking claim of the verse.

options.text: A private matter with no spiritual significance.
options.note: The verse explicitly ties treatment of the poor to how one treats God Himself.

options.text: Something God is indifferent toward.
options.note: The strong language, taunts their Maker, shows deep divine concern, not indifference.

options.text: A concern only for religious leaders to address.
options.note: The proverb addresses this as a matter for any person, not a specialized religious duty.

quiz.q: What does verse 34 say determines a nation's exaltation or disgrace?

options.text: Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a disgrace to any people.
options.note: This is the exact statement of the verse.

options.text: Military strength alone.
options.note: The verse names righteousness and sin, not military power, as decisive.

options.text: The size of a nation's population only.
options.note: Population is mentioned nearby, verse 28, but this specific verse names righteousness and sin as the true determining factors.

options.text: Wealth accumulated by its rulers.
options.note: The verse's concern is moral, righteousness versus sin, not the wealth of rulers.

quiz.q: How does verse 31's link between the poor and their Maker anticipate Christ's teaching?

options.text: Christ teaches that whatever is done for the least of His brothers is done for Him personally, deepening this proverb's claim.
options.note: Matthew 25:40, 45 makes this connection directly and personally in Christ.

options.text: It has no connection to anything Christ later taught.
options.note: Matthew 25 draws on exactly this kind of identification between God and the poor.

options.text: It shows that only the poor themselves are accountable to God.
options.note: The verse addresses how others treat the poor, not a special accountability placed on the poor themselves.

options.text: It applies only to ancient Israelite civil law, with no further relevance.
options.note: This understates how directly the New Testament develops and personalizes this very principle in Christ.

questions: Verse 1 pictures a wise woman actively building her house and a foolish one tearing hers down with her own hands. What are you actively building, or unintentionally tearing down, in your own home or family right now?

Verse 12 warns that a way can feel completely right and still lead to death. Is there a decision or direction in your life that feels right to you but that you have not actually tested against Scripture or wise counsel?

Verse 21 calls kindness to the poor a blessing, and verse 31 says oppressing them taunts God Himself. How does your treatment of those with less than you reflect, or fail to reflect, how you would treat God directly?
Verse 29 says a patient man has great understanding, while a quick-tempered man promotes folly. Where has impatience recently led you to say or do something foolish?
Christ says whatever is done for the least of His brothers is done for Him. Who is someone vulnerable in your life this week that you could serve as though you were serving Christ Himself?

translationNotes.note: This verse is difficult in the Hebrew, and translations vary; the BSB rendering, fools mock the making of amends, captures the general sense of fools despising reconciliation that upright people value.

The phrase 'a refuge even in death' can also be understood as trusting in his integrity even in the face of death, both readings pointing to the righteous having a confidence that outlasts mortal danger.
